extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write and read mathematical proofs (introductory 'Book of Proof' readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing clear, correct direct proofs and related combinatorial arguments (division/pigeonhole, combinatorial proofs, case analysis) at the undergraduate level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must be understandable and convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of a theorem is a written verification that shows that the theorem is definitely and unequivocally true. A proof should be understandable and convincing to anyone who has the requisite background and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguity; ensure all mathematical words, phrases and symbols used in the theorem and proof have agreed meanings. The proof should be written so that readers with the stated background can follow and be persuaded by the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exact, unambiguous definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions must give an exact, unambiguous explanation of the meaning of mathematical words or phrases (e.g., even: n = 2a for some integer a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase definitions clearly (the book uses conditional phrasing by convention but interprets them biconditionally). Use definitions when they apply in proofs. Mark defined terms consistently (the book uses boldface) and rely on them to transform assumptions into usable algebraic statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for direct proof (assume P, show Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: For conditional statements of the form 'If P, then Q,' the standard direct-proof strategy is: begin by assuming P, then deduce Q using logic, definitions, and standard facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minimal skeleton is 'Suppose P.' ... 'Therefore Q.' Fill in intermediate steps that logically transform P into Q. You do not need to consider cases where P is false because the implication is automatically true there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit use of definitions in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When an assumption invokes a definition (e.g., 'x is odd'), replace it immediately with the defining algebraic form (e.g., x = 2a + 1) to enable algebraic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice clarifies the route from hypothesis to conclusion; use fresh variable names when introducing existential witnesses from definitions to avoid conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable naming discipline (avoid reuse/conflicts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reuse variable names in different contexts in a way that creates ambiguity (e.g., avoid reusing 'c' when it already denotes something else).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying definitions that introduce existential variables, choose new letters (example: use d and e when a,b,c already appear). Consistent and non-conflicting notation improves clarity and prevents logical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accepted facts and previously proved results appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to use standard arithmetic/algebraic facts (commutativity, distributivity, division algorithm, unique prime factorization) and previously proved propositions as building blocks in new proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite or rely on such facts when needed. Recognize which results are accepted without proof in the current context and which need citation or proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proof: count the same set two ways
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove identities combinatorially, show that two different expressions both count the same collection of combinatorial objects; conclude the expressions are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide the counting task into cases or complementary choices (e.g., whether an element is included), apply multiplication/addition principles, and match constructions to algebraic terms (examples: Pascal's identity, binomial coefficient symmetries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division principle / Pigeonhole principle usage and formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: When n objects are placed into k boxes, at least one box contains at least ceiling(n/k) objects and at least one box contains at most floor(n/k) objects. Consequences: if n>k some box has more than one object; if n<k some box is empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model problems by placing items into appropriately defined 'boxes' (including averaging arguments). Use ceiling/floor rounding as required. Examples: birthdays, gumball color guarantee, geometric partitioning to bound areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis when expressions behave differently
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement's truth depends on mutually exclusive conditions (e.g., parity, sign, membership), split the proof into cases and show the statement holds in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label cases clearly (Case 1, Case 2, ...). Work each case to completion; then conclude the overall statement. Example: parity-based proofs where n even vs n odd give different algebraic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation conventions: Proof markers and QED
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin proofs with a marker such as 'Proof.' and end them with a terminating symbol (e.g., a square or '∎'). Proofs may be written line-by-line for clarity or in paragraph form once polished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's often helpful in drafting to write the first ('Suppose P') and last ('Therefore Q') lines first and then fill in the middle. Scratch work and sketches are normal; polish the final write-up for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: prove equalities by double inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two nonnegative quantities m and n are equal, one effective method is to show m ≤ n and n ≤ m (or m < n and n < m where appropriate), thereby concluding m = n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use different logical routes for each direction if needed. Example: lcm identity proved by showing each side is a least/smallest multiple and bounding the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality manipulation caution (squaring, square roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating inequalities one must respect domain/monotonicity constraints: e.g., squaring both sides preserves order only when both sides are nonnegative; taking square roots requires positive sides to avoid reversing inequalities improperly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either reduce to a previously proved monotonicity result (take square roots after proving both sides are nonnegative) or explicitly justify each manipulation step. Examples: deducing 2√(xy) < x + y by squaring after showing positivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting principles: multiplication/addition/subtraction/division
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the basic counting principles (multiplication rule for sequences of independent choices, addition rule for disjoint alternatives, subtraction for complementary counting, and division for counting up to symmetry) when solving counting problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model choices explicitly (e.g., boxes for division/pigeonhole arguments); account for identical items, ordering constraints, or capacity limits properly. Examples include permutations with repeated letters and distributing identical balls into boxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and notation of divisibility and related number-theoretic terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise definitions for divisibility (a | b iff b = a c for some integer c), greatest common divisor, least common multiple, prime/composite, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the definitions directly in proofs to obtain equations that can be algebraically manipulated (e.g., from a|b and b|c deduce b = a d and c = b e and hence c = a(de)). Note domain caveats (e.g., gcd(0,0) excluded by convention).
